entry.sum: A metric space is a set $X$ with a distance function $d$ that is zero exactly when the two points coincide (and positive otherwise), symmetric, and satisfies the triangle inequality. Once distance is available, convergence, open and closed sets, continuity and Cauchy sequences all make sense, whether the points are vectors, functions, strings or $p$-adic integers. In a complete metric space every contraction has a unique fixed point (Banach's theorem), which is a basic tool for proving that equations have solutions.
key: d(x, y) \ge 0,\quad d(x, y) = 0 \iff x = y,\quad d(x, y) = d(y, x),\quad d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)
x_n \to x \iff d(x_n, x) \to 0, \qquad U \text{ open} \iff \forall x \in U\ \exists r > 0:\ B(x, r) \subseteq U
X \text{ complete},\ d(Tx, Ty) \le q\, d(x, y),\ 0 \le q < 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; \exists!\, x^* \in X:\ Tx^* = x^*
entry.why: Metric spaces let one theory of limits cover numbers, vectors and functions at once; the contraction principle is the core of the standard proofs of the existence theorem for differential equations and of the inverse function theorem, and it explains the convergence of many numerical iterations.

links.note: The $p$-adic distance $|x - y|_p = p^{-v_p(x - y)}$ makes integers close when their difference is divisible by a high power of $p$; completing $\mathbb Q$ for it gives the $p$-adic numbers.
The Hamming distance between strings measures how many symbols differ, and error-correcting codes are sets of strings that are far apart in this metric.
Changing the metric on $\mathbb R^2$ changes the shape of circles, from the round Euclidean disc to the diamond of the taxicab metric and the square of the maximum metric.

refs: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces
Kaplansky, Set Theory and Metric Spaces

blocks.body:
The definition of convergence in [[seq-limits]] uses only one thing about real numbers: the distance $|a - b|$. So the same definition should work wherever there is a sensible distance. How far apart are the functions $\sin x$ and $x$ on $[0, 1]$? How different are the words "metric" and "matrix"? When are two integers close? Each question has a natural answer, and each answer satisfies the same three rules.

A metric space is any set equipped with a distance obeying those rules. The payoff is economy: one proof about metric spaces is at once a theorem about $\mathbb R^n$, about spaces of functions, and about $p$-adic numbers. This lesson sets up the language and proves the contraction principle, the simplest and most widely used existence theorem in analysis.

blocks.title: Metric space
A gallery of metrics
blocks.body:
- The real line with $d(x, y) = |x - y|$, and $\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean distance $d_2(\mathbf x, \mathbf y) = \sqrt{\sum (x_i - y_i)^2}$; its triangle inequality comes from [[cauchy-schwarz]].
- On $\mathbb R^n$ also $d_1(\mathbf x, \mathbf y) = \sum |x_i - y_i|$ (the taxicab metric) and $d_\infty(\mathbf x, \mathbf y) = \max_i |x_i - y_i|$. In the plane the unit "circle" $\{\mathbf x : d(\mathbf x, \mathbf 0) = 1\}$ is a round circle for $d_2$, a diamond with vertices $(\pm1, 0), (0, \pm1)$ for $d_1$, and a square with vertices $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$ for $d_\infty$.
- The discrete metric on any set: $d(x, y) = 1$ if $x \ne y$, and $0$ if $x = y$.
- The Hamming distance between strings of length $n$: the number of positions where they differ. Changing one string into another one position at a time shows the triangle inequality.
- The sup metric on the set $C[a, b]$ of continuous functions on $[a, b]$: $d(f, g) = \max_{a \le x \le b} |f(x) - g(x)|$. Two functions are close when their graphs are uniformly close. For example $d(\sin x, x) = 1 - \sin 1 \approx 0.159$ on $[0, 1]$, since $x - \sin x$ is increasing there.
- The $p$-adic metric on $\mathbb Z$ for a prime $p$: $d(x, y) = p^{-v_p(x - y)}$, where $v_p(m)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $m$ and $d(x, x) = 0$. Here $1$ and $1 + 5^{10}$ are very close in the $5$-adic metric.

Any subset of a metric space is again a metric space with the same $d$: for instance $\mathbb Q$, or the interval $(0, 1)$.

blocks.title: Convergence, open sets and continuity
blocks.body:
Everything from [[seq-limits]] transfers word for word. A sequence $(x_n)$ in $X$ converges to $x$ if $d(x_n, x) \to 0$, that is, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_n, x) < \varepsilon$ for $n \ge N$. Limits are unique, by the same triangle inequality argument as before.

The open ball of radius $r > 0$ around $x$ is $B(x, r) = \{y \in X : d(x, y) < r\}$. A set $U \subseteq X$ is open if around each of its points there is a ball inside $U$, and a set $F$ is closed if its complement is open. Open balls are open sets: if $y \in B(x, r)$, put $s = r - d(x, y) > 0$; for $z \in B(y, s)$ the triangle inequality gives $d(x, z) < d(x, y) + s = r$, so $B(y, s) \subseteq B(x, r)$. A set $F$ is closed exactly when it contains the limit of every convergent sequence of its points (a short exercise with the definitions).

A map $f : X \to Y$ between metric spaces is continuous at $a$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $d_Y(f(x), f(a)) < \varepsilon$ whenever $d_X(x, a) < \delta$. Equivalently, $x_n \to a$ implies $f(x_n) \to f(a)$, just as for real functions in [[continuity]]. A map with $d(f(x), f(y)) \le K\,d(x, y)$ for a constant $K > 0$ (a Lipschitz map) is continuous: take $\delta = \varepsilon / K$.

Different metrics on the same set can give different convergent sequences. In the discrete metric, $x_n \to x$ only if $x_n = x$ for all large $n$. In the $2$-adic metric, $2^n \to 0$, since $d(2^n, 0) = 2^{-n}$.

blocks.title: Cauchy sequence and completeness
blocks.body:
A sequence $(x_n)$ in a metric space is a Cauchy sequence if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m, x_n) < \varepsilon$ for all $m, n \ge N$. The space is complete if every Cauchy sequence in it converges to a point of the space.

Every convergent sequence is Cauchy. Completeness asks for the converse: the space has no holes. $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^n$ are complete (by the Cauchy criterion, coordinate by coordinate), and so is every closed subset of a complete space. $\mathbb Q$ is not complete (decimal approximations of $\sqrt 2$), and neither is $(0, 1)$ (the sequence $\frac1n$, $n \ge 2$, is Cauchy but its limit is missing).

The space $C[a, b]$ of real-valued continuous functions on a closed bounded interval, with the sup metric, is complete. If $(f_n)$ is Cauchy in this metric, then for each $x$ the numbers $f_n(x)$ form a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb R$, so they converge to a number $f(x)$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, take $N$ with $|f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $x$ and all $m, n \ge N$; letting $m \to \infty$ gives $|f_n(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon$ for all $x$, so the convergence is uniform. Finally, a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (proved in [[uniform-convergence]]), so $f \in C[a, b]$ and $d(f_n, f) \to 0$.

blocks.title: Banach fixed-point theorem
blocks.body:
Let $(X, d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space and $T : X \to X$ a contraction: there is $q$ with $0 \le q < 1$ and $d(Tx, Ty) \le q\,d(x, y)$ for all $x, y \in X$. Then $T$ has exactly one fixed point $x^*$. Moreover, for any starting point $x_0$ the iterates $x_{n + 1} = Tx_n$ converge to $x^*$, with
$$d(x_n, x^*) \le \frac{q^n}{1 - q}\, d(x_0, x_1).$$

Each step shrinks distances by the factor $q$, so by induction $d(x_{k + 1}, x_k) \le q^k d(x_1, x_0)$. For $m > n$, the triangle inequality along the path $x_n, x_{n + 1}, \dots, x_m$ gives
$$d(x_n, x_m) \le \sum_{k = n}^{m - 1} q^k d(x_1, x_0) \le \frac{q^n}{1 - q}\, d(x_1, x_0).$$
The right side tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$, so $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, and by completeness it converges to some $x^* \in X$.

$T$ is Lipschitz, hence continuous, so $Tx^* = \lim Tx_n = \lim x_{n + 1} = x^*$. If $y^*$ is another fixed point, then $d(x^*, y^*) = d(Tx^*, Ty^*) \le q\,d(x^*, y^*)$, which forces $d(x^*, y^*) = 0$ because $q < 1$.

For the error estimate, fix $n$ and let $m \to \infty$ in $d(x_n, x_m) \le \frac{q^n}{1 - q}d(x_1, x_0)$. Since $|d(x_n, x_m) - d(x_n, x^*)| \le d(x_m, x^*) \to 0$, the bound passes to the limit as $d(x_n, x^*) \le \frac{q^n}{1 - q}d(x_1, x_0)$.

blocks.title: A bounded metric
blocks.body: Show that $\rho(x, y) = \dfrac{|x - y|}{1 + |x - y|}$ is a metric on $\mathbb R$, that $\rho < 1$, and that it has the same convergent sequences as the usual metric.
blocks.solution:
Let $\varphi(t) = \frac{t}{1 + t} = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + t}$ for $t \ge 0$. It is increasing, $\varphi(0) = 0$, $\varphi(t) > 0$ for $t > 0$, and $\varphi(t) < 1$. So the first two rules for $\rho = \varphi(|x - y|)$ are clear. For the triangle inequality we need two facts. First, $\varphi$ is subadditive: for $a, b \ge 0$,
$$\varphi(a + b) = \frac{a}{1 + a + b} + \frac{b}{1 + a + b} \le \frac{a}{1 + a} + \frac{b}{1 + b} = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b).$$
Second, $|x - z| \le |x - y| + |y - z|$ and $\varphi$ is increasing, so
$$\rho(x, z) = \varphi(|x - z|) \le \varphi(|x - y| + |y - z|) \le \varphi(|x - y|) + \varphi(|y - z|) = \rho(x, y) + \rho(y, z).$$
Finally $\rho(x_n, x) \to 0$ if and only if $|x_n - x| \to 0$, because $\varphi(t) \le t$, and $t = \frac{\varphi(t)}{1 - \varphi(t)}$ is small when $\varphi(t)$ is. So "bounded" is not a property of a set alone; it depends on the metric.

blocks.title: A strange but useful metric
blocks.body: In the $p$-adic metric on $\mathbb Z$ show the strong triangle inequality $d(x, z) \le \max(d(x, y), d(y, z))$, and deduce that every triangle is isosceles. Then show that $1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^{n - 1} \to -1$ in the $2$-adic metric.
blocks.solution:
If $p^a$ divides $x - y$ and $p^b$ divides $y - z$, then $p^{\min(a, b)}$ divides their sum $x - z$. So $v_p(x - z) \ge \min(v_p(x - y), v_p(y - z))$, and since $t \mapsto p^{-t}$ is decreasing, $d(x, z) \le \max(d(x, y), d(y, z))$. This is stronger than the triangle inequality, so $d$ is a metric (the other two rules are immediate).

Isosceles triangles: suppose $d(x, y) < d(y, z)$. Then $d(x, z) \le d(y, z)$ by the strong inequality, and also $d(y, z) \le \max(d(y, x), d(x, z))$, where the maximum cannot be $d(y, x) < d(y, z)$; so $d(y, z) \le d(x, z)$. Hence $d(x, z) = d(y, z)$: the two longest sides are always equal.

For the series, $1 + 2 + \cdots + 2^{n - 1} = 2^n - 1$, and $d(2^n - 1, -1) = 2^{-v_2(2^n)} = 2^{-n} \to 0$. So in the $2$-adic world the "divergent" sum $1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots$ converges to $-1$, as the formula $\frac{1}{1 - 2}$ for a geometric series suggests. See [[p-adic-valuation]].

blocks.title: Solving an equation by iteration
blocks.body: Show that the equation $\cos x = x$ has exactly one solution in $[0, 1]$, and estimate how many iterations of $x_{n + 1} = \cos x_n$ starting from $x_0 = 1$ guarantee an error below $10^{-6}$.
blocks.solution:
The interval $X = [0, 1]$ is closed in $\mathbb R$, hence complete. Since $\cos$ decreases on $[0, 1]$, it maps $X$ into $[\cos 1, 1] \subseteq X$. By the [[mvt]], $|\cos x - \cos y| = |\sin \xi|\,|x - y|$ for some $\xi$ between $x$ and $y$, so $|\cos x - \cos y| \le q|x - y|$ with $q = \sin 1 \approx 0.8415 < 1$. So $\cos$ is a contraction of $X$, and Banach's theorem gives exactly one fixed point $x^* \approx 0.739085$ in $[0, 1]$.

With $d(x_0, x_1) = 1 - \cos 1 \approx 0.4597$, the error bound $\frac{q^n}{1 - q} \cdot 0.4597$ drops below $10^{-6}$ once $n \ge 87$. In practice convergence is faster: near the fixed point the contraction factor is $\sin x^* \approx 0.674$, and $32$ iterations already suffice. The theorem's bound is guaranteed, not sharp.

blocks.title: A functional equation solved in a space of functions
blocks.body: Show that there is exactly one continuous function $f : [0, 1] \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) = x + \frac12 f(x^2)$ for all $x$, and find it.
blocks.solution:
Work in $X = C[0, 1]$ with the sup metric, which is complete. Define $(Tf)(x) = x + \frac12 f(x^2)$. If $f$ is continuous, so is $Tf$, so $T : X \to X$. For $f, g \in X$,
$$|(Tf)(x) - (Tg)(x)| = \tfrac12 |f(x^2) - g(x^2)| \le \tfrac12\, d(f, g)$$
for every $x$, because $x^2 \in [0, 1]$. So $d(Tf, Tg) \le \frac12 d(f, g)$: $T$ is a contraction, and the equation $Tf = f$ has exactly one continuous solution.

To find it, iterate from $f_0 = 0$: $f_1 = x$, $f_2 = x + \frac{x^2}{2}$, $f_3 = x + \frac{x^2}2 + \frac{x^4}{4}$, and in general $f_n(x) = \sum_{k = 0}^{n - 1} \frac{x^{2^k}}{2^k}$. These converge in the sup metric to
$$f(x) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{x^{2^k}}{2^k} = x + \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^4}{4} + \frac{x^8}{8} + \cdots,$$
and indeed $x + \frac12 f(x^2) = x + \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{x^{2^{k + 1}}}{2^{k + 1}} = f(x)$. Here the points of the metric space are functions, and the fixed point is a function.

blocks.body:
- Completeness depends on the metric, not only on the set, and not even only on which sequences converge. The interval $(0, 1)$ is not complete with $|x - y|$. But with $\rho(x, y) = |h(x) - h(y)|$, where $h(x) = \tan(\pi x - \frac\pi2)$ maps $(0, 1)$ bijectively and continuously onto $\mathbb R$ with continuous inverse, it is an exact copy of $\mathbb R$ and is complete, although both metrics have the same convergent sequences.
- Open and closed are not opposites. In $\mathbb R$, $[0, 1)$ is neither, and $\mathbb R$ itself is both. In the discrete metric every set is both open and closed.
- Shrinking distances is not enough for a fixed point; the factor must be a uniform $q < 1$. The map $T(x) = x + \frac1x$ on the complete space $[1, \infty)$ satisfies $|Tx - Ty| < |x - y|$ for $x \ne y$, but has no fixed point.
- Closed and bounded does not imply compact in a general metric space; see [[compactness]].
- Checking the triangle inequality only on examples proves nothing; it must hold for all triples.

The next step is [[compactness]], which generalises the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem. The sup metric on functions is the setting of [[uniform-convergence]]; the existence theorem for [[ode-first|differential equations]] is the contraction principle applied to Picard's integral operator on such a space. Metrics coming from norms and [[inner-products]] turn [[vector-spaces]] into normed spaces, and the $L^p$ spaces ($1 \le p \le \infty$) of [[lebesgue]] integration are complete metric spaces of this kind. The $p$-adic metric leads to the $p$-adic numbers and [[hensel|Hensel's lemma]], which is itself a contraction argument in disguise.

1. Prove that $d_\infty(\mathbf x, \mathbf y) = \max_i |x_i - y_i|$ is a metric on $\mathbb R^n$, and sketch its unit ball in the plane.
2. Prove that in a metric space every convergent sequence is Cauchy.
3. Show that in the discrete metric a sequence converges if and only if it is eventually constant, and that every subset is open.
4. Show that $T(x) = \frac x2 + \frac1x$ maps $[1, 2]$ into itself and is a contraction there. What is its fixed point?

entry.sum: A metric space $K$ is compact if every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence converging to a point of $K$; equivalently, every cover of $K$ by open sets has a finite subcover. In $\mathbb R^n$ the compact sets are exactly the closed and bounded ones (Heine–Borel). Continuous real functions on a nonempty compact set are bounded, attain a maximum and a minimum, and are uniformly continuous.
key: K \text{ compact} \iff \text{every sequence in } K \text{ has a subsequence converging in } K \quad (K \text{ a metric space})
K \subseteq \mathbb R^n:\quad K \text{ compact} \iff K \text{ closed and bounded}
f : K \to \mathbb R \text{ continuous},\ K \ne \varnothing \text{ compact} \;\Longrightarrow\; \exists\, a, b \in K:\ f(a) = \max_K f,\ f(b) = \min_K f
entry.why: Compactness is what guarantees that optimisation problems have solutions and that local estimates can be made global; it is behind the extreme value theorem, the integrability of continuous functions, and countless existence proofs.

links.note: The compactness theorem of first-order logic (a set of sentences has a model if every finite subset does) is named for the same finite-subcover phenomenon and is equivalent to the compactness of a certain topological space.
Compactness arguments such as König's lemma pass from finite to infinite statements, for example from $k$-colourings of every finite subgraph to a $k$-colouring of an infinite graph.

Compactness of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^n$ shows that all norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent and that a symmetric matrix attains its largest eigenvalue as the maximum of $\mathbf x^T A \mathbf x$ on the sphere.

blocks.body:
Does the function $f(x) = x$ have a largest value? On $[0, 1]$ yes, at $x = 1$. On $(0, 1)$ no: it gets as close to $1$ as you like but never reaches it. On $\mathbb R$ no: it is unbounded. The function $\frac1x$ on $(0, 1]$ is not even bounded. Whether a maximum exists depends on the domain, and the property of $[0, 1]$ that the other domains lack is compactness.

Compactness is the precise sense in which a set behaves like a finite one: no sequence can wander off to infinity or escape towards a missing point. This lesson works in [[metric-spaces]] and uses [[continuity]] in its sequential form: $f$ is continuous at $a$ exactly when $x_n \to a$ implies $f(x_n) \to f(a)$.

blocks.title: Compact set
blocks.body:
A metric space $K$ (or a subset $K$ of a metric space, with the same distance) is compact if every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence that converges to a point of $K$.

In words: however you choose infinitely many points of $K$, they must pile up somewhere inside $K$.

blocks.title: Examples and the open-cover definition
blocks.body:
- Every closed bounded interval $[a, b]$ is compact. A sequence in $[a, b]$ is bounded, so by the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem in [[seq-limits]] it has a convergent subsequence; its limit lies in $[a, b]$ because $a \le x_n \le b$ is preserved by limits.
- $(0, 1]$ is not compact: the sequence $\frac1n$ converges to $0$, so every subsequence also converges to $0$, which is not in the set.
- $\mathbb R$ is not compact: the sequence $1, 2, 3, \dots$ has no convergent subsequence, since convergent sequences are bounded.
- Every finite set is compact: some point is repeated infinitely often, giving a constant subsequence.
- $\{0\} \cup \{\frac1n : n \in \mathbb N\}$ is compact: a sequence either takes some value infinitely often, or it has a subsequence along which the index of $\frac1n$ tends to infinity, and then that subsequence converges to $0$.

There is a second, equivalent definition. An open cover of $K$ is a collection of open sets whose union contains $K$. For metric spaces, $K$ is compact in the sequential sense if and only if every open cover of $K$ has a finite subcollection that still covers $K$. We quote this theorem without proof (Munkres's Topology proves it, for example). It depends on the metric: for general topological spaces the two notions are different, and there the open-cover form is taken as the definition of compactness. The cover of $(0, 1)$ by the intervals $(\frac1n, 1)$, $n \ge 2$, shows the failure for a non-compact set: any finitely many of them have union $(\frac1N, 1)$ for the largest $N$ used, which misses $\frac{1}{2N}$. The open-cover form is the right tool for turning local information into global information.

blocks.title: Compact sets are closed and bounded
blocks.body:
(a) In any metric space, a compact set is closed and bounded.

(b) Heine–Borel: a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ (with the Euclidean metric) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

(a) Let $K$ be compact. Closed: let $x_n \in K$ with $x_n \to x$. Some subsequence converges to a point $y \in K$; but every subsequence of $(x_n)$ also converges to $x$, so by uniqueness of limits $x = y \in K$. Bounded: the empty set is bounded, so let $K \ne \varnothing$; if $K$ were unbounded, fix $p \in K$ and choose $x_n \in K$ with $d(x_n, p) > n$. Any subsequence $x_{n_k}$ has $d(x_{n_k}, p) > n_k \to \infty$, so it is unbounded and cannot converge, a contradiction.

(b) One direction is (a). Conversely let $K \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be closed and bounded, and let $(\mathbf x_m)$ be a sequence in $K$. Each coordinate sequence is bounded. By Bolzano–Weierstrass choose a subsequence along which the first coordinates converge; from it choose a further subsequence along which the second coordinates also converge; after $n$ steps we have a subsequence along which every coordinate converges, hence which converges in $\mathbb R^n$. Its limit lies in $K$ because $K$ is closed.

blocks.title: Extreme value theorem
blocks.body: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and $f : K \to \mathbb R$ continuous. Then $f$ is bounded and there are points $a, b \in K$ with $f(b) \le f(x) \le f(a)$ for all $x \in K$.

Bounded above: otherwise choose $x_n \in K$ with $f(x_n) > n$. A subsequence $x_{n_k}$ converges to some $x \in K$, and by continuity $f(x_{n_k}) \to f(x)$. But $f(x_{n_k}) > n_k \to \infty$, and a convergent sequence is bounded: contradiction.

So $M = \sup_{x \in K} f(x)$ exists by completeness of $\mathbb R$ (see [[real-numbers]]). By the approximation property of the supremum choose $x_n \in K$ with $f(x_n) > M - \frac1n$. A subsequence converges to some $a \in K$, and $f(x_{n_k}) \to f(a)$. Since $M - \frac{1}{n_k} < f(x_{n_k}) \le M$, the squeeze rule gives $f(a) = M$. The minimum is obtained by applying this to $-f$.

blocks.title: Images and uniform continuity
blocks.body:
Continuous images of compact sets are compact: if $f : K \to Y$ is continuous and $(y_n)$ is a sequence in $f(K)$, write $y_n = f(x_n)$, pick a subsequence $x_{n_k} \to x \in K$, and then $y_{n_k} \to f(x)$. The extreme value theorem is the special case $Y = \mathbb R$, since a compact subset of $\mathbb R$ is closed and bounded and therefore contains its supremum and infimum.

A function $f : X \to \mathbb R$ is uniformly continuous if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is one $\delta > 0$ that works at every point: $d(x, y) < \delta$ implies $|f(x) - f(y)| < \varepsilon$. On $(0, 1]$ the continuous function $\frac1x$ is not uniformly continuous, since near $0$ the required $\delta$ shrinks to nothing. On compact sets this cannot happen.

blocks.title: Heine–Cantor theorem
blocks.body: Every continuous function $f : K \to \mathbb R$ on a compact metric space $K$ is uniformly continuous.

Suppose not. Then there is an $\varepsilon > 0$ for which no $\delta$ works; taking $\delta = \frac1n$ we get points $x_n, y_n \in K$ with $d(x_n, y_n) < \frac1n$ but $|f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \ge \varepsilon$. A subsequence $x_{n_k}$ converges to some $a \in K$. Then also $y_{n_k} \to a$, because $d(y_{n_k}, a) \le d(y_{n_k}, x_{n_k}) + d(x_{n_k}, a) \to 0$. By continuity at $a$, both $f(x_{n_k})$ and $f(y_{n_k})$ tend to $f(a)$, so their difference tends to $0$, contradicting $|f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k})| \ge \varepsilon$.

blocks.title: Heine–Borel fails in infinite dimensions
blocks.body: In the space $C[0, 1]$ of continuous functions with the sup metric $d(f, g) = \max |f - g|$, let $B = \{f : d(f, 0) \le 1\}$ be the closed unit ball. Show that $B$ is closed and bounded but not compact.
blocks.solution:
$B$ is bounded by definition, and closed because if $f_n \to f$ with $\max|f_n| \le 1$, then $|f(x)| = \lim |f_n(x)| \le 1$ for each $x$.

Now consider $f_n(x) = x^n$, all in $B$. Suppose a subsequence $f_{n_k}$ converged in the sup metric to some $g \in C[0, 1]$. Sup convergence implies convergence at each point, $f_{n_k}(x) \to g(x)$. But $x^{n_k} \to 0$ for $0 \le x < 1$ and $1^{n_k} = 1$, so $g(x) = 0$ for $x < 1$ and $g(1) = 1$. Such a $g$ is not continuous, a contradiction. So no subsequence converges, and $B$ is not compact.

One can see the obstruction directly with the functions $x^{2^k}$. For $j < k$, substituting $t = x^{2^j}$ gives $d(x^{2^j}, x^{2^k}) = \max_{t \in [0, 1]} (t - t^{2^{k - j}}) \ge \frac12 - \frac14 = \frac14$ (take $t = \frac12$), so these functions stay at least $\frac14$ apart and no subsequence of them is Cauchy. (Consecutive powers do get close: $d(x^n, x^{n + 1}) \to 0$.) The lesson: Heine–Borel is a theorem about $\mathbb R^n$, not about metric spaces in general.

blocks.title: Nearest points exist
blocks.body: Show that for every nonempty closed set $F \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and every point $\mathbf p$, some point of $F$ is nearest to $\mathbf p$. Find the distance from $(0, 2)$ to the parabola $y = x^2$.
blocks.solution:
$F$ itself may be unbounded, so first cut it down. Fix any $\mathbf q_0 \in F$ and let $r = |\mathbf p - \mathbf q_0|$. Points of $F$ farther than $r$ from $\mathbf p$ cannot be nearest, so it suffices to minimise over $F' = F \cap \{\mathbf q : |\mathbf q - \mathbf p| \le r\}$. This set is nonempty, closed (an intersection of two closed sets) and bounded, so compact by Heine–Borel. The function $\mathbf q \mapsto |\mathbf q - \mathbf p|$ is continuous, so it attains a minimum on $F'$, and that minimum is the distance from $\mathbf p$ to $F$.

For the parabola, which is closed since it is the zero set of the continuous function $y - x^2$, the squared distance from $(0, 2)$ to $(x, x^2)$ is $x^2 + (x^2 - 2)^2 = t^2 - 3t + 4$ with $t = x^2 \ge 0$. This is smallest at $t = \frac32$, with value $\frac74$. So the nearest points are $\left(\pm\sqrt{3/2}, \frac32\right)$ and the distance is $\frac{\sqrt7}{2}$. Existence came first, from compactness; the calculus only located the point.

blocks.title: A fixed-point theorem without a contraction constant
blocks.body: Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and $f : K \to K$ a map with $d(f(x), f(y)) < d(x, y)$ for all $x \ne y$. Prove that $f$ has exactly one fixed point.
blocks.solution:
The map $f$ is continuous, since $d(f(x), f(y)) \le d(x, y)$. Consider $g(x) = d(x, f(x))$. It is continuous, because by the triangle inequality $|g(x) - g(y)| \le d(x, y) + d(f(x), f(y)) \le 2d(x, y)$. By the extreme value theorem $g$ attains its minimum at some $a \in K$.

If $f(a) \ne a$, apply the hypothesis to the distinct points $a$ and $f(a)$:
$$g(f(a)) = d(f(a), f(f(a))) < d(a, f(a)) = g(a),$$
contradicting the minimality of $g(a)$. So $f(a) = a$. If $b \ne a$ were another fixed point, then $d(a, b) = d(f(a), f(b)) < d(a, b)$, which is absurd.

Compare with the [[metric-spaces]] lesson, where $x + \frac1x$ on $[1, \infty)$ shrinks all distances but has no fixed point: that space is complete but not compact. On $[0, 1]$ the map $\sin x$ sends $[0, 1]$ into $[0, \sin 1] \subseteq [0, 1]$ and satisfies the hypothesis (by the [[mvt]], since $\cos \xi < 1$ for $0 < \xi \le 1$) but no uniform $q < 1$ works near $0$, so Banach's theorem does not apply; compactness still gives the unique fixed point $0$.

blocks.body:
- Closed and bounded implies compact in $\mathbb R^n$ (and in every finite-dimensional normed space), but not in a general metric space. It fails for the unit ball of $C[0, 1]$, for $\mathbb N$ with the discrete metric, and for $[0, 2] \cap \mathbb Q$ inside $\mathbb Q$, where a sequence of rationals tending to $\sqrt 2$ has no limit in the space.
- Compactness is a property of the set with its metric, not of how it sits in a bigger space. Closedness is relative: $(0, 1)$ is closed as a subset of itself but is not compact.
- The extreme value theorem needs both hypotheses. $\frac1x$ on $(0, 1]$ (domain not compact) and the discontinuous function equal to $x$ on $[0, 1)$ and $0$ at $1$ (compact domain) both fail to attain a maximum.
- In a general metric space, compact means complete and totally bounded: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, finitely many balls of radius $\varepsilon$ cover the set. Bounded is much weaker; the unit ball of $C[0, 1]$ cannot be covered by finitely many balls of radius $\frac18$, since the functions $x^{2^k}$ are pairwise at distance at least $\frac14$.

Compactness is how existence is proved: constrained extrema in [[lagrange-multipliers]], the maximum of a Rayleigh quotient in the [[spectral-theorem]], and Riemann integrability of continuous functions in [[riemann-integral]], via uniform continuity. In function spaces the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem characterises compact sets of continuous functions, a companion to [[uniform-convergence]]. Measure theory ([[lebesgue]]) starts from the compactness of $[a, b]$, which forces any cover of $[a, b]$ by open intervals to have total length at least $b - a$. In combinatorics, compactness arguments pass from finite to infinite configurations ([[infinite-combinatorics]], [[ramsey]]), and in logic the compactness theorem plays the same role for models.

1. Prove that a closed subset of a compact metric space is compact, and that a finite union of compact sets is compact.
2. Prove that if $K$ is compact and $f : K \to Y$ is continuous and injective, then $f^{-1} : f(K) \to K$ is continuous.
3. Give a bounded continuous function on $(0, 1)$ that attains neither its supremum nor its infimum.
4. Show that $\{(x, y) : x^4 + y^4 \le 1\}$ is compact, and conclude that $x + y$ has a maximum on it.
